title: Theseus and the Thread
source: Theseus and the Minotaur, Bulfinch's Mythology, 1867 (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theseus

start.text: You are Theseus at the maze gate. Ariadne offers you a ball of thread.

n1.text: You tie the thread to the gate and walk in. The tunnels split.

n3.text: The hum leads to the Minotaur, sitting alone behind a stone pillar.

n2.text: Inside, every wall looks alike. You find a crossing with old chalk marks.

e1.text: The wide tunnel ends in a dusty hall of statues. You follow the thread back out and try another day, a little wiser. The end.

e2.text: You stand tall and speak calmly. The weary Minotaur backs away, and you lead the young people of Athens out along the thread. The end.

e3.text: You slip past and find a stair up to a sunny garden. You rest there, then follow the thread home, glad you were patient. The end.

e4.text: The chalk leads in circles until Ariadne hears you call and lowers a rope through a skylight. Next time, you promise, you take the thread. The end.

e5.text: You walk back out and thank Ariadne. With the thread in hand you try again the next day, and this time you find your way. The end.

title: Odysseus and the Giant
source: Odysseus and Polyphemus, the Odyssey (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphemus

start.text: You are Odysseus. Your ship lands by a huge cave full of sheep.

n1.text: The giant shepherd, Polyphemus, rolls a stone across the door and asks your name.

n3.text: He chuckles at the odd name. At dawn he lets his sheep out to graze.

n2.text: Hours pass and your friends have not come back. The night is long.

e1.text: Polyphemus listens, tired of loud guests. He grumbles, then shares his cheese and lets you leave if you promise to sail on quietly. The end.

e2.text: Clinging beneath the woolly sheep, you and your friends pass the giant's patting hand unseen. You run to the ship, laughing. The end.

e3.text: While the giant naps, you dig a gap beside the stone. By noon you all squeeze through and hurry to the ship. The end.

e4.text: You find your friends on the far beach, picking figs and lost in a song. Together you sail on, glad you looked for them. The end.

e5.text: You sail until dawn, but the empty deck feels wrong. You turn back, find everyone safe, and all go home together. The end.

title: Pandora's Jar
source: Pandora, Hesiod's Works and Days (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandora

start.text: You are Pandora. A gift from the gods sits at home: a sealed jar.

n1.text: Days pass. The jar hums softly. Your husband Epimetheus is curious too.

n3.text: He says the jar may hold troubles, and perhaps something good too.

n2.text: You lift the lid a crack. Little grey worries buzz out into the room.

e1.text: You bury the jar under an olive tree. The world stays calm, though you sometimes wonder what it held. The end.

e2.text: Worries fly out, but Hope rises last and sits on your shoulder. Together you learn to face troubles with hope. The end.

e3.text: You carry the jar to the temple. Pleased with your patience, the gods grant you a garden that never withers. The end.

e4.text: A few worries escape, but Hope stays inside. You let her out gently, and she helps people through hard days. The end.

e5.text: Many worries drift into the world, but Hope floats out last, a small glow that helps everyone cope. The end.

title: Jack and the Beanstalk
source: Jack and the Beanstalk, Joseph Jacobs, English Fairy Tales, 1890 (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_and_the_Beanstalk

start.text: You are Jack. A stranger at market offers magic beans for your thin cow.

n1.text: Overnight a beanstalk climbs past the clouds. A castle stands at the top.

n3.text: A giant's wife gives you bread. Then thundering footsteps shake the floor.

n2.text: You sell her milk instead. A baker offers you a job beside her warm ovens.

e1.text: Through the window you see a giant counting gold and snoring. You tiptoe back down, glad of your own small, warm home. The end.

e2.text: From the bread bin you watch the giant doze. You take a small golden hen, slide down the stalk, and your family never goes hungry. The end.

e3.text: You slide down the stalk, safe but empty-handed. Next morning the beans sprout again, and you try once more, braver. The end.

e4.text: You learn to bake, and your mother is proud. Years later you plant the last bean, just to see what grows. The end.

e5.text: The stranger is gone, but you find one bean on the road. You plant it, and a small green sprout begins to climb. The end.

title: The Piper of Hamelin
source: The Pied Piper of Hamelin, Grimm, Deutsche Sagen, 1816 (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pied_Piper_of_Hamelin

start.text: You are a piper in Hamelin. The town is full of rats. The mayor promises gold.

n1.text: Your tune draws the rats to the river. The mayor frowns at the price.

n3.text: He offers half the gold. Children gather by the gate to hear your pipe.

n2.text: Your trap catches a few rats a night. The mayor grows impatient.

e1.text: You leave the gold behind. The town is rat-free, and the ashamed mayor sends the full pay after you with a note of thanks. The end.

e2.text: You take half and the town cheers. Neighbours add the rest and a feast, and you stay a year to teach children music. The end.

e3.text: You play a dancing tune. The children follow you up a green hill, and the sorry mayor hurries to pay in full. All dance home. The end.

e4.text: Week by week the rats thin out and the town learns patience. The mayor thanks you with a cottage and fair pay. The end.

e5.text: You fetch your pipe at last and play a calm tune. The rats follow you to the river, and the mayor pays at once. The end.

title: Momotaro and the Peach
source: Momotaro, Yei Theodora Ozaki, Japanese Fairy Tales, 1908 (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momotar%C5%8D

start.text: You are Momotaro, born from a peach. Trouble stirs on a far island. You pack dumplings.

n1.text: A dog begs for a dumpling and offers to join you.

n3.text: A monkey and a pheasant join too. The island rises ahead.

n2.text: The elder hands you a banner. Kindness, she says, is your best tool.

e1.text: You walk on alone and reach the shore tired. A fisher takes you home, and you decide a friend would have eased the trip. The end.

e2.text: You, the dog, monkey and pheasant arrive at dawn. The surprised demons return the stolen treasure and promise to behave. The end.

e3.text: You rush ahead and the gate slams. Your friends catch up and talk the demons into peace over a shared meal. The end.

e4.text: With the banner raised you sail. The demons see your calm face and agree to talk, and treasure returns to the villages. The end.

e5.text: You stay and help mend the village fences. Word of your kindness spreads, and the demons later send a letter of apology. The end.

title: King Midas's Wish
source: King Midas, from Ovid's Metamorphoses, with the daughter from Hawthorne's A Wonder-Book, 1852 (public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midas

start.text: You are King Midas. The god Dionysus offers you one wish for your kindness.

n1.text: All you touch turns to gold: your chair, your cup, even your breakfast bread.

n3.text: Your meal is gold. Your daughter runs to hug you, and you stop, afraid to touch her.

n2.text: Dionysus smiles. Wisdom will show you what to do with good fortune.

e1.text: You ask Dionysus to undo the gift. He sends you to wash in the river Pactolus, and the golden touch flows away. The end.

e2.text: You run to Dionysus, who sends you to the river Pactolus. You wash, your touch turns plain again, and you hug your daughter. The end.

e3.text: Your daughter brings thick gloves and guides you to the river Pactolus, where the golden touch washes off. You embrace her. The end.

e4.text: You rule fairly. Fields grow and people thrive, and you are remembered for gentle judgment, not for gold. The end.

e5.text: You travel quietly, learn from farmers and sailors, and bring home simple ideas that help your whole kingdom. The end.

title: The Dancing Princesses
source: The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Grimms' Fairy Tales (Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 1815, public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Dancing_Princesses

start.text: You are a soldier. The king's twelve daughters wear out their shoes each night. Why?

n1.text: An old woman gives you a cloak that hides you, and warns: sip nothing offered.

n3.text: You follow the princesses down secret stairs to a silver forest and boats.

n2.text: A maid whispers that stairs under the eldest's bed lead somewhere strange.

e1.text: Without the cloak you are noticed and politely sent back up. You thank the princesses for the walk and leave kindly. The end.

e2.text: You watch them dance till dawn, then tell the king. The princesses, relieved that the spell is spotted, thank you. The end.

e3.text: You snap a silver twig and they hear it. Surprised, they agree to show the king, and the spell breaks. All is forgiven. The end.

e4.text: You find the dance hall and join in. Your kindness lifts the spell, and the princesses sleep soundly for the first time. The end.

e5.text: The king laughs, then follows the stairs himself. Together you break the spell with a shared feast instead of a dance. The end.

title: Rumpelstiltskin's Name
source: Rumpelstiltskin, Grimms' Fairy Tales (Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 1812, public domain), retold: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumpelstiltskin

start.text: You are a miller's daughter. A strange little man offers to spin straw into gold.

n1.text: He spins again and asks for your first child as payment. The room goes silent.

n3.text: Years later he returns. He gives you three days to guess his name.

n2.text: You tell the king the truth: you cannot spin gold. He listens kindly.

e1.text: He bows and vanishes. You tell the king the truth, and he values your honesty above all the gold in the world. The end.

e2.text: Your maid overheard a little man singing his name by a fire. You say it, Rumpelstiltskin, and he leaves, free of the deal. The end.

e3.text: In the woods you hear a little man singing his name, Rumpelstiltskin, by a fire. You say it next day, and he stamps off. The end.

e4.text: You work in the king's mill for honest wages and become its manager. You never need magic gold again. The end.

e5.text: You leave and open a bakery by the river. Customers come from miles away for your warm bread. The end.
